title: CAC vs LTV Explained (With Formulas and a Worked Example)
meta_description: CAC is what it costs to acquire a customer; LTV is what they're worth over time. See both formulas, a worked example, and what LTV:CAC ratio is healthy.
primary_keyword: cac vs ltv explained
content_md:
# CAC vs LTV Explained

**CAC**, short for Customer Acquisition Cost, is how much money a company spends, on average, to win one new paying customer. **LTV**, short for Lifetime Value (sometimes called CLV), is how much revenue that same customer is expected to bring in over the entire time they stay with the company. When you compare the two as a ratio — LTV to CAC — you get an answer to one of the most important questions any subscription business can ask: are we making more money from each customer than it costs us to win them in the first place?

## Quick facts

- **CAC formula:** total money spent on sales and marketing, divided by the number of new customers won in that same time period.
- **LTV formula (simple version):** the average amount a customer pays each period, multiplied by how long they typically stay.
- Most healthy subscription businesses aim for an **LTV to CAC ratio of about 3 to 1, or higher**.
- A ratio below 1 to 1 means the company is losing money on every new customer, even before counting other costs.
- A ratio above about 5 to 1 can actually be a warning sign too — it may mean the company isn't spending enough on growth.

## The formulas

**CAC:**
```
CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / Number of New Customers Acquired
```

**LTV (simple version):**
```
LTV = Average Revenue Per Customer × Average Customer Lifespan
```

**LTV (a more accurate version, adjusted for profit margin):**
```
LTV = (Average Revenue Per Customer × Gross Margin %) × Average Customer Lifespan
```
Gross margin is the percentage of revenue left after subtracting the direct cost of delivering the product or service — it makes the LTV number closer to actual profit, not just raw revenue.

## A worked example

Picture a business software company that sells invoicing tools. We'll call it "Ledgerly," the same made-up company from our other examples, to keep the numbers easy to follow. Last quarter, Ledgerly spent $120,000 on sales and marketing, and won 200 new customers.

**CAC = $120,000 ÷ 200 = $600 per customer**

Ledgerly's average customer pays $50 a month, stays subscribed for 24 months on average, and the company keeps 80% of that revenue as gross margin (the rest covers the direct cost of running the service).

**LTV = ($50 × 0.80) × 24 = $960 per customer**

**LTV to CAC ratio = $960 ÷ $600 = 1.6 to 1**

This is below the healthy target of about 3 to 1. In plain terms, Ledgerly is spending too much to win each customer, compared to what that customer is actually worth. Before spending more on growth, the company should either lower its CAC (find cheaper, more efficient ways to reach customers) or raise its LTV (keep customers longer, or get more revenue from each one).

## What counts as a "good" ratio

| LTV to CAC ratio | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Below 1 to 1 | Losing money on every new customer — this can't continue |
| 1 to 1 up to 3 to 1 | Weak — acquisition costs are eating too much of each customer's value |
| 3 to 1 up to 5 to 1 | Healthy — the range most subscription businesses aim for |
| Above 5 to 1 | Efficient, but possibly a sign the company could safely spend more to grow faster |

## Why this matters to a product manager, not just to finance

CAC and LTV aren't only a finance or marketing concern. Every product decision that helps customers stay longer (see [retention rate](/product-metrics/what-is-retention-rate-vs-churn-rate)), get started faster (see [activation rate](/product-metrics/what-is-activation-rate-in-product-analytics)), or spend more over time (see [expansion revenue](/product-led-growth/what-is-expansion-revenue-and-how-to-drive-it)) directly raises LTV. And anything that makes onboarding or self-serve sign-up smoother can directly lower CAC. A product manager who can say "this change raised our LTV to CAC ratio from 2.1 to 2.8" is making an argument that any executive will immediately understand — far more convincing than usage numbers alone.

## Common mistakes when calculating CAC and LTV

- **Leaving out costs that belong in CAC.** Total sales and marketing spend should include salaries, ad spend, tools, and content costs — not just ad spend alone. Counting only paid ads makes CAC look artificially low.
- **Using revenue instead of margin-adjusted revenue for LTV.** As shown above, raw revenue overstates how valuable a customer really is, because it ignores the cost of actually serving them.
- **Comparing CAC and LTV across very different customer segments as if they were one number.** A $50-a-month customer and a $5,000-a-month enterprise customer have completely different CAC and LTV profiles — blending them into one average ratio can hide serious problems in one segment.
- **Calculating LTV once and never updating it.** Customer lifespan and revenue per customer both change as a product matures — an LTV number from two years ago can be dangerously out of date if pricing or retention has shifted since then.

## How LTV:CAC changes as a company grows

Early-stage companies often have a lower, sometimes even negative, LTV:CAC ratio, and that's not automatically a bad sign — it can simply mean the company hasn't yet had enough time to see how long customers actually stick around, so the LTV side of the equation is underestimated. What matters is the trend: a healthy company should see its ratio improve over time as the product and retention improve, even if the very first year or two of data looks weak. A ratio that stays flat or gets worse over several quarters is the real warning sign, not a low number in year one.

## FAQ

**What's a good CAC payback period?**
Most healthy subscription companies aim to earn back their CAC within 12 to 18 months of a customer signing up. A faster payback period means less financial risk while the company keeps spending on growth.

**Does LTV include the cost of actually serving the customer?**
The margin-adjusted version of the LTV formula does, because it multiplies revenue by gross margin percentage. This gives a more accurate picture than simply using raw revenue, which would overstate how valuable a customer really is.

**How is LTV to CAC different from a normal return-on-investment (ROI) calculation?**
A typical ROI calculation usually looks at a single, shorter period. LTV to CAC looks at the entire relationship with a customer, which fits subscription businesses better, since the value from one customer builds up over years, not from a single purchase.

**Can a brand-new startup calculate LTV accurately before it has years of data?**
Not precisely. Early-stage companies usually estimate it using the first few months of retention data they do have, and refine the number as more real data comes in — rather than waiting years to get a "true" answer.

**Should CAC include the cost of the sales team, or just marketing?**
It should include both. A complete CAC calculation adds together every cost involved in winning a new customer — marketing spend, sales salaries and commissions, and any tools or software used specifically for acquisition — divided by the number of new customers won in that period.

**Is a high LTV:CAC ratio always a good thing?**
Not necessarily. As mentioned above, a very high ratio (often cited as above 5 to 1) can mean a company is being too cautious with its growth spending and could likely afford to acquire customers faster without hurting its unit economics — so "higher is always better" isn't quite the right way to read this number.

# The CIRCLES Method for Product Sense Questions

CIRCLES is a step-by-step structure, developed by Lewis Lin, for answering product design and [product sense interview questions](/pm-interview-prep/product-sense-interview-questions-explained) — questions like "design a product for X" or "how would you improve Y." The acronym stands for **C**omprehend the situation, **I**dentify the customer, **R**eport customer needs, **C**ut through prioritization, **L**ist solutions, **E**valuate trade-offs, and **S**ummarize your recommendation — a full sequence for organizing an otherwise open-ended, potentially rambling answer.

## Quick facts

- CIRCLES stands for: **C**omprehend, **I**dentify the customer, **R**eport needs, **C**ut through prioritization, **L**ist solutions, **E**valuate trade-offs, **S**ummarize.
- It's a more detailed, step-by-step version of the general structured approach described in [Product Sense Interview Questions Explained](/pm-interview-prep/product-sense-interview-questions-explained).
- Created by Lewis Lin, a well-known interview coach in the product management space.
- The framework works best as a mental checklist to guide genuine reasoning, not a script to recite word for word.

## The seven steps, explained

| Step | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **C**omprehend the situation | Clarify the question — what product, what goal, any ambiguity worth resolving upfront |
| **I**dentify the customer | Define specifically who you're designing for |
| **R**eport customer needs | Identify the real problems or needs this customer segment has |
| **C**ut through prioritization | Decide which need to focus on, and explain why |
| **L**ist solutions | Generate multiple possible solutions for the prioritized need |
| **E**valuate trade-offs | Weigh the pros and cons of your top solution options |
| **S**ummarize your recommendation | State your final recommendation clearly, with brief reasoning |

## A full worked example: "Design a product for busy parents"

**Comprehend:** "To clarify — are we designing a brand-new product, or a feature for an existing one? I'll assume this is a new, standalone product concept."

**Identify the customer:** "I'll focus on parents of young children, roughly ages 2-8, who are juggling full-time work alongside parenting responsibilities."

**Report needs:** "Likely needs include: coordinating schedules across school, activities, and childcare; reducing the mental load of tracking many small logistics; and finding brief pockets of quality time despite limited availability."

**Cut through prioritization:** "I'd focus on reducing the mental load of coordination, since this seems like a frequent, high-friction pain point that affects daily life directly, more so than the other needs identified."

**List solutions:** "A few options: a shared family calendar with automatic reminders, a delegation tool for splitting logistics tasks between co-parents or caregivers, or an AI assistant that proactively surfaces upcoming logistics conflicts before they become last-minute problems."

**Evaluate trade-offs:** "A shared calendar is simple to build but is already a crowded space with many existing tools. The AI assistant is more differentiated but harder to build well and requires trust in its proactive suggestions. The delegation tool addresses a specific, less-served need — coordinating between multiple caregivers — with less existing competition."

**Summarize:** "I'd recommend starting with the delegation tool, since it addresses a specific, underserved need with less direct competition, and could expand toward the AI assistant concept once we have real usage data and trust established with users."

## Why the "Cut through prioritization" step matters so much

A common weakness in product sense answers is identifying several plausible customer needs, then trying to design a solution addressing all of them simultaneously — producing an unfocused, sprawling answer. The CIRCLES method's explicit prioritization step forces a candidate to make a real, defensible choice about what matters most, then focus the rest of the answer there — mirroring the real skill product managers need on the job, where focus and prioritization matter more than generating an exhaustive list of possibilities.

## How CIRCLES compares to a general structured approach

CIRCLES is essentially a more detailed, explicitly named version of the general structured approach (clarify, identify problems, prioritize, propose solutions, measure success) covered in [Product Sense Interview Questions Explained](/pm-interview-prep/product-sense-interview-questions-explained). Some candidates find CIRCLES's explicit seven-step structure easier to remember and apply consistently; others find a looser, more general structure feels more natural and less rigid in the moment. Either approach works — what matters most is genuinely organizing your answer with clear reasoning, not which specific named framework you use.

## Common mistakes when using CIRCLES

- **Reciting the acronym steps mechanically without genuinely reasoning through each one.** Interviewers can tell when a candidate is following a memorized script rather than actually thinking through the specific question.
- **Spending too much time on Comprehend and Identify, leaving little time for the more important Cut through prioritization and Evaluate trade-offs steps.**
- **Skipping the Evaluate trade-offs step entirely**, jumping straight from listing solutions to a recommendation without showing the reasoning that led there.
- **Treating every step as equally important to spend time on**, rather than adjusting emphasis based on what the specific question actually calls for.

## FAQ

**Who created the CIRCLES method?**
Lewis Lin, an interview coach well known in the product management interview preparation space, developed and popularized this specific framework.

**Should I memorize the CIRCLES acronym before an interview?**
It can help as a mental checklist to make sure you cover the key steps, but reciting it rigidly or announcing each step by name during the actual interview often feels unnatural — better to internalize the underlying structure and let it guide a genuine, conversational answer.

**Is CIRCLES only useful for "design a product for X" questions, or does it work for "how would you improve Y" questions too?**
It works for both — the same underlying structure (clarify, identify the customer and needs, prioritize, generate and evaluate solutions, recommend) applies whether you're designing something new or improving an existing product.

**How is CIRCLES different from just using common sense to structure an answer?**
CIRCLES formalizes what strong, naturally structured answers already tend to do — it's most useful for candidates who find open-ended interview questions genuinely difficult to organize on the spot, giving them an explicit checklist to fall back on under interview pressure.

title: Cohort Analysis Explained for Beginners (With Example)
meta_description: Cohort analysis groups users by when they started, so you can see how their behavior changes over time. See how it works, with a worked example.
primary_keyword: cohort analysis explained for beginners
content_md:
# Cohort Analysis Explained for Beginners

Cohort analysis groups users by something they share — most commonly, the week or month they first signed up — and then tracks how each group's behavior changes over time. Instead of looking at one blended, overall number (like "our retention rate is 60%"), cohort analysis lets you compare, for example, how well January's new users stuck around versus how well June's new users stuck around, which reveals whether the product is actually getting better or worse at keeping people, something a single overall average can hide.

## Quick facts

- A **cohort** is simply a group of users who share a starting point in time — usually the month or week they signed up.
- Cohort analysis is most commonly used to study **retention** — what percentage of a cohort is still active after 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, and so on.
- The output is usually shown as a table or chart, with one row per cohort and one column per time period since signup — this specific layout is often called a cohort retention table, or sometimes described visually as a "cohort waterfall."
- Cohort analysis reveals trends that a single blended average number hides, since averaging across all users mixes old, established users with brand-new ones.
- It's a foundational tool for understanding both [retention/churn](/product-metrics/what-is-churn-rate-and-how-to-reduce-it) and how well onboarding or product changes are actually working over time.

## Why a single overall number isn't enough

If a product simply reports "60% of our users are active this month," that number blends together long-time loyal users with brand-new signups from last week — two very different groups with very different behavior. A product could have terrible new-user retention while still showing a healthy-looking overall active user number, simply because its established, loyal base is large and stable. Cohort analysis fixes this by isolating each starting group and tracking it on its own, so a change in new-user quality shows up clearly instead of getting hidden in a blended average.

## A worked example: a simple cohort retention table

Imagine a habit-tracking app looking at retention by monthly signup cohort:

| Signup month | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 4 | Week 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | 100% | 62% | 41% | 30% |
| February | 100% | 65% | 44% | 33% |
| March | 100% | 58% | 35% | 22% |
| April | 100% | 70% | 50% | 38% |

Reading this table: every cohort starts at 100% in their first week (everyone was active when they signed up, by definition). Looking across the rows shows how retention decays over time for each specific group. Looking down the columns reveals a trend: March's cohort retained noticeably worse than February's at every time point, while April's cohort retained the best of all four months. This immediately raises a useful question — what happened in March that hurt new-user retention, and what happened in April that helped it? A single blended monthly retention number would never have surfaced this specific, actionable pattern.

## How to actually use cohort analysis to improve a product

The real value of cohort analysis comes from connecting a change in cohort behavior to something the team actually did. If March's cohort retained poorly, the next step is investigating what changed that month — a pricing change, a confusing new onboarding flow, a bug, or a shift in what kind of user was being acquired through marketing. If April's cohort retained noticeably better, and the team shipped a new onboarding flow that month, that's a strong, testable signal the new flow genuinely helped — far more convincing than an anecdote or a gut feeling, because it's backed by a clear before-and-after comparison across similar groups of users.

## Cohorts beyond just signup date

While signup-date cohorts are the most common, cohorts can be grouped by almost anything meaningful: which acquisition channel brought them in (cohort by marketing source), which pricing plan they started on, or which version of an onboarding flow they experienced. Grouping by acquisition channel, for example, can reveal that users from one channel retain far better than users from another — useful information for deciding where to invest marketing spend, not just how to improve the product itself.

## Common mistakes when doing cohort analysis

- **Comparing cohorts of very different sizes without noting it.** A cohort of 20 users behaves much more erratically than a cohort of 2,000 — a single unusual user can swing a small cohort's numbers dramatically, which can be misread as a meaningful trend when it's really just noise.
- **Only looking at retention, and never other cohort-based metrics.** Cohort analysis works for revenue, feature adoption, and referral behavior too, not just whether someone stays active — limiting it to retention alone misses other useful patterns.
- **Not connecting a cohort trend to an actual explanation.** Spotting that March's cohort retained worse is only half the job — the real value comes from investigating and confirming why, then acting on it.
- **Drawing conclusions from cohorts that are still too new to have long-term data.** A cohort that signed up two weeks ago can't yet tell you anything about 3-month retention — comparing incomplete cohort data to fully mature cohorts produces misleading conclusions.

## FAQ

**What's the difference between cohort analysis and a retention rate?**
[Retention rate](/product-metrics/what-is-retention-rate-vs-churn-rate) is usually a single, blended number for a given period. Cohort analysis breaks that same underlying idea down by starting group, over time, which reveals trends and patterns a single blended retention number can't show on its own.

**How many cohorts do you need before the analysis becomes meaningful?**
There's no fixed number, but comparing at least 3-4 cohorts of reasonably similar size makes trends easier to distinguish from random noise — a single cohort, or comparing wildly different-sized cohorts, makes patterns much harder to trust.

**Can cohort analysis be used for revenue, not just user retention?**
Yes — revenue cohort analysis tracks how much revenue each signup group generates over time, which is especially useful for understanding [LTV](/product-metrics/cac-vs-ltv-explained) patterns and whether newer customers are becoming more or less valuable over time compared to older ones.

**What tools are commonly used to build cohort analysis?**
Most product analytics platforms (like Amplitude, Mixpanel, or a company's own internal data warehouse and BI tool) have built-in cohort analysis features, since this is one of the most common and valuable ways product teams study user behavior over time.

title: Common Mistakes in Customer Discovery
meta_description: The most common ways customer discovery goes wrong — from leading questions to pitching too early — and how to actually avoid each one.
primary_keyword: common mistakes in customer discovery
content_md:
# Common Mistakes in Customer Discovery

Customer discovery fails quietly more often than it fails obviously — a team runs interviews, feels like they've done real research, and still ends up building the wrong thing, because the process itself was subtly flawed. These are the most common, recurring ways this happens, and what to do instead.

## Quick facts

- The most common mistake is **pitching the solution too early**, before genuinely understanding whether the underlying problem is real.
- **Leading questions** are the second most common flaw — subtly steering interviewees toward confirming what the team already believes.
- Talking only to **easy-to-reach people** (friends, existing enthusiastic customers) skews findings toward a non-representative picture.
- See the full process this guide's mistakes apply to in [Customer Discovery Process for New Products](/product-discovery/customer-discovery-process-for-new-products).

## Mistake 1: Pitching the solution before validating the problem

Many teams jump straight into describing their product idea and gauging reaction, without first confirming the underlying problem is real and significant enough to matter. This produces polite, often falsely encouraging feedback — people are generally kind and will find something positive to say about almost any idea presented to them directly. **Fix:** run problem-focused interviews first, without mentioning your solution, and look for evidence the problem itself is real and painful before introducing what you're building.

## Mistake 2: Asking leading questions

Questions like "wouldn't it be great if you could do X?" invite agreement rather than honest, independent reaction — most people will politely agree rather than push back, even if they don't genuinely feel strongly about it. **Fix:** use neutral, [open-ended questions](/product-discovery/how-to-write-good-user-interview-questions) grounded in specific past behavior, and watch carefully for language in your own questions that hints at the answer you're hoping to hear.

## Mistake 3: Only talking to easy-to-reach people

Friends, colleagues, and existing enthusiastic customers are convenient to talk to, but they're rarely representative of your broader target market — they may already be biased favorably toward you, or simply unrepresentative of how a genuine stranger in your target market would react. **Fix:** deliberately recruit participants who don't already have a relationship with you or your company, even though this takes more effort than reaching out to your existing network.

## Mistake 4: Treating polite interest as strong validation

"That sounds interesting" or "I'd probably use that" costs a person nothing to say, and is a weak predictor of real future behavior. **Fix:** look for evidence that costs the person something real — a pre-order, a genuine time commitment, an honest description of an existing painful workaround — rather than treating verbal enthusiasm alone as meaningful validation.

## Mistake 5: Stopping after too few conversations

A single enthusiastic conversation, or even three or four, isn't enough to confirm a genuine, widespread pattern — it could easily be coincidence, or reflect an unusual, unrepresentative person. **Fix:** continue until you see a clear, repeated pattern across a meaningful number of independent conversations, not just an early promising signal.

## Mistake 6: Ignoring or explaining away negative signals

It's tempting to dismiss discouraging feedback as coming from "the wrong type of user" or "someone who just doesn't get it yet," rather than genuinely engaging with what it might reveal. **Fix:** treat negative or lukewarm signals as seriously as positive ones — they often contain the most valuable, course-correcting information, precisely because they're uncomfortable to hear.

## Mistake 7: Not separating the underlying problem from the requested solution

Customers often describe a specific solution they want, when the real underlying need might be better addressed a different way entirely. **Fix:** always dig into the "why" behind a request — what are they actually trying to accomplish — rather than taking a literal feature request at face value.

## Mistake 8: Running discovery as a one-time phase instead of an ongoing practice

Teams sometimes treat customer discovery as something done once, early on, then set aside once building begins. **Fix:** maintain some form of [continuous discovery](/product-discovery/continuous-discovery-habits-for-product-teams) even after initial validation, since customer needs and market conditions keep evolving after the initial research phase ends.

## FAQ

**Which of these mistakes is the most damaging?**
Pitching the solution before validating the problem is often considered the most damaging, since it can lead a team to build a well-executed solution to a problem that was never actually significant or real in the first place — the most fundamental flaw a discovery process can have.

**Can these mistakes happen even with an experienced product team?**
Yes — even experienced teams fall into these patterns, especially under time pressure or when they're personally excited about a specific idea, which makes them more likely to unconsciously seek confirming rather than genuinely testing evidence.

**How can a team check whether they're making these mistakes without realizing it?**
Having someone outside the immediate team review interview questions and a sample of interview recordings or notes can catch leading language, premature solution-pitching, or other issues that are hard to notice from inside the process.

**Is it possible to fully eliminate bias from customer discovery?**
Not entirely — some degree of bias is difficult to fully eliminate, but being deliberately aware of these common failure patterns, and building in genuine checks against them (like neutral question review), meaningfully reduces their impact on the resulting decisions.

title: Continuous Discovery Habits for Product Teams
meta_description: Continuous discovery means talking to customers every week, not just during occasional research pushes. See the core habits and how to build them.

content_md:
# Continuous Discovery Habits for Product Teams

Continuous discovery, a concept popularized by Teresa Torres, means talking to customers on a regular, ongoing basis — often weekly — rather than doing research only in occasional, large pushes before a big decision. The core belief: product teams that maintain regular, small touchpoints with real customers develop sharper intuition and catch problems earlier than teams that only research sporadically, right before a major initiative.

## Quick facts

- The core habit is **weekly customer touchpoints** — small, regular conversations, not occasional large research projects.
- Continuous discovery pairs closely with the [Opportunity Solution Tree](/product-frameworks/opportunity-solution-tree-explained), which gets updated as ongoing discovery surfaces new understanding.
- The goal is building sustained customer intuition across the whole team, not just running research as a one-off project phase.
- Popularized by Teresa Torres, a well-known product discovery coach.

## Why weekly touchpoints matter more than occasional big research pushes

Occasional, large research projects tend to happen only before major decisions, meaning a team's customer understanding can become stale between those pushes — priorities and customer needs shift continuously, but the team's knowledge doesn't update unless another big research effort is deliberately scheduled. Weekly touchpoints, even small ones, keep customer understanding continuously fresh, letting a team catch shifting needs and emerging problems much earlier than they would through periodic, large-batch research alone.

## The core continuous discovery habits

| Habit | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Weekly customer conversations** | A regular cadence of interviews or touchpoints, even just one per week, rather than sporadic research bursts |
| **Small, focused research questions** | Each conversation doesn't need to cover everything — a specific, narrow question per touchpoint is often more useful |
| **Updating the opportunity solution tree regularly** | New understanding from ongoing conversations feeds back into a living, evolving picture, not a static one-time artifact |
| **Involving the whole team, not just researchers** | Product managers, designers, and sometimes engineers directly participate in customer conversations, not just a dedicated research function |
| **Synthesizing findings quickly and sharing broadly** | Insight from each conversation gets captured and shared promptly, rather than sitting unprocessed |

## Why involving the whole team matters

A common pattern in occasional, project-based research is that findings get filtered through a dedicated researcher or a single product manager, then summarized for the rest of the team — losing nuance and immediacy in the process. Continuous discovery encourages broader team involvement in actual customer conversations, on the theory that direct exposure builds much stronger, more durable intuition than reading someone else's research summary — a designer who's personally heard a customer's frustration firsthand tends to design around it more effectively than one who's only read about it secondhand.

## How to actually build this habit on a team that doesn't have it yet

Starting continuous discovery doesn't require an elaborate research program from day one — a realistic starting point is committing to just one customer conversation per week, rotating who conducts it across the team, with a simple, consistent process for quickly capturing and sharing what was learned. Building the habit itself matters more initially than optimizing the process — a consistent, if imperfect, weekly cadence beats an occasional, more elaborate research effort that doesn't sustain itself over time.

## How continuous discovery connects to prioritization

Regular, ongoing customer contact directly feeds into better-informed prioritization decisions — a team that's continuously talking to customers has fresher, more current evidence to weigh when making calls with frameworks like [RICE](/product-frameworks/rice-framework-explained-with-example), rather than relying on research that may be many months old and increasingly disconnected from current customer reality. This is part of why continuous discovery and the [Opportunity Solution Tree](/product-frameworks/opportunity-solution-tree-explained) are often taught together — the tree is the living artifact that continuous discovery keeps updated and accurate.

## Common mistakes when building continuous discovery habits

- **Treating it as a project with a defined end, rather than an ongoing team habit.** The value comes specifically from sustained, continuous practice, not a temporary initiative that fades after a few months.
- **Only having a dedicated researcher conduct customer conversations**, missing the broader team's direct exposure and the intuition it builds.
- **Trying to cover too much in each weekly touchpoint**, rather than keeping individual conversations focused on a specific, narrow question.
- **Not maintaining a living artifact (like an opportunity solution tree) to actually capture and use the accumulating insight.** Without this, ongoing conversations risk generating insight that's never systematically captured or acted on.

## FAQ

**How much time does continuous discovery actually require each week?**
It varies, but many teams start with as little as one 30-45 minute customer conversation per week, plus a short synthesis session — a modest, sustainable time commitment rather than a significant new project.

**Is continuous discovery only relevant for B2C products with many users to talk to?**
No — it applies to B2B products too, though B2B teams often need to be more deliberate about maintaining a rotating pool of willing customer contacts, given typically smaller customer bases than consumer products.

**Does continuous discovery replace the need for larger, occasional research projects?**
Not entirely — larger, more structured research efforts still have value for deeper, more comprehensive questions; continuous discovery complements this by keeping the team's baseline understanding fresh between those larger efforts, rather than replacing them entirely.

**Who should be responsible for scheduling and running weekly customer conversations?**
Practices vary, but many teams rotate this responsibility across product, design, and sometimes engineering, rather than assigning it permanently to one person — this distributes the direct customer exposure and its intuition-building benefit more broadly across the team.

title: Core PM vs Platform PM vs Growth PM: The Differences
meta_description: Core, platform, and growth product manager roles focus on different things. See exactly what each one owns and how to know which fits you.
primary_keyword: core pm vs platform pm vs growth pm
content_md:
# Core PM vs Platform PM vs Growth PM

As companies grow, the generic "product manager" title often splits into more specialized roles focused on different parts of the product. A **core PM** owns a primary, customer-facing part of the product. A **platform PM** owns internal systems and infrastructure that other teams build on top of. A **growth PM** focuses specifically on the metrics driving acquisition, activation, and retention, often running frequent experiments rather than owning a large feature area.

## Quick facts

- **Core PM**: owns a primary, customer-facing product area — the features most users interact with directly.
- **Platform PM**: owns internal, foundational systems — APIs, infrastructure, shared services other teams depend on.
- **Growth PM**: focuses on specific funnel metrics (acquisition, activation, retention) through frequent, often smaller experiments.
- These specializations typically emerge once a company is large enough to need dedicated ownership across genuinely different types of product work.
- See how this compares to the technical specialization specifically in [What Is a Technical Product Manager](/product-management/what-is-a-technical-product-manager).

## Side-by-side comparison

| | Core PM | Platform PM | Growth PM |
|---|---|---|---|
| What they own | A primary customer-facing product area | Internal systems/infrastructure used by other teams | Specific funnel metrics (acquisition, activation, retention) |
| Who the "customer" often is | End users directly | Other internal teams or external developers | Users at a specific funnel stage |
| Typical work rhythm | Roadmap-driven, feature-focused | Architecture and reliability-focused, longer planning horizons | Rapid, frequent experimentation |
| Success measured by | Feature adoption, customer satisfaction | System reliability, internal team velocity/satisfaction | Movement on specific funnel metrics |

## What a core PM actually does

A core PM owns the primary product experience most users interact with — think the main features of a consumer app, or the central workflow of a B2B tool. Their work tends to follow a more traditional product management rhythm: understanding customer needs, building a roadmap, and shipping features that directly shape the customer experience. This is often the role people picture when they hear "product manager," and it's frequently the starting point before someone specializes further.

## What a platform PM actually does

A platform PM owns infrastructure and internal systems — APIs, shared services, internal developer tools — that other product teams build on top of, rather than owning a customer-facing feature directly. Their "customers" are often other engineers or product teams within the company, or external developers if the platform includes a public API. This role requires strong technical fluency (see [Technical Product Manager](/product-management/what-is-a-technical-product-manager)) since the work involves genuine architecture and system-design trade-offs, and success is often measured in reliability and how effectively other teams can build on the platform, rather than direct end-user satisfaction.

## What a growth PM actually does

A growth PM focuses narrowly and intensely on specific metrics along the user funnel — how people discover the product, how quickly they activate, and what keeps them retained. Rather than owning a broad feature area, growth PMs typically run a high volume of smaller, fast experiments (a different onboarding flow, a pricing page test, a referral incentive) and rely heavily on data to decide what to try next. This role suits people who enjoy fast iteration cycles and are comfortable with a large share of experiments not working, since growth work is inherently a high-volume, high-failure-rate discipline by design.

## How to know which specialization fits you

If you're energized by deep customer conversations and shaping the core experience people interact with daily, core PM fits well. If you enjoy technical architecture problems and working primarily with other engineers rather than end customers, platform PM is a strong fit — particularly for people with an engineering background. If you're drawn to fast, data-driven experimentation and are comfortable with most individual experiments failing as long as the overall program moves metrics, growth PM fits well.

## Can you move between these specializations?

Yes, and it's common — many product managers start in a core PM role (often the most common entry point) and later specialize into platform or growth work as they discover which type of problem-solving genuinely energizes them, or as a company's specific needs create an opening. The underlying PM fundamentals (prioritization, communication, customer understanding) transfer across all three; what differs is the specific domain knowledge and working rhythm each specialization requires.

## Common mistakes when thinking about these roles

- **Assuming one specialization is more prestigious or senior than the others.** They're different types of work, not different levels of the same job — a senior platform PM and a senior core PM are both senior, just in different domains.
- **Taking a platform PM role without genuine technical interest or fluency.** This specialization specifically requires comfort with deep technical trade-off conversations — a poor fit here creates real friction with engineering.
- **Expecting growth PM work to feel like traditional feature-driven product management.** The rapid experimentation rhythm and high failure rate of individual tests is a genuinely different working style that doesn't suit everyone.
- **Assuming these categories are rigid or universal.** Company-specific role definitions vary, and some companies use different names or blend these responsibilities differently than this general framework suggests.

## FAQ

**Which of these three roles is easiest to break into first?**
Core PM is generally the most common entry point, since it doesn't require the specific technical depth platform PM needs, or the data/experimentation-heavy skill set growth PM requires — though this varies by company and individual background.

**Does a growth PM need strong technical/data skills?**
Yes, generally more than a typical core PM — comfort reading and interpreting experiment data, understanding statistical significance, and working closely with data teams are core parts of the role.

**Is platform PM only relevant at large companies?**
It's most common at larger companies with enough internal complexity to need dedicated platform ownership, though smaller companies building genuinely platform-oriented products (like a developer tools company) can have platform PM roles even at an earlier stage.

**Can a single person hold responsibilities across more than one of these specializations?**
Yes, especially at smaller companies — one product manager might handle both core and growth responsibilities before the company is large enough to justify fully separate, dedicated roles for each specialization.

**Platform PM**: owns internal, foundational systems — APIs, infrastructure, shared services other teams depend on.
**Growth PM**: focuses on specific funnel metrics (acquisition, activation, retention) through frequent, often smaller experiments.
These specializations typically emerge once a company is large enough to need dedicated ownership across genuinely different types of product work.
See how this compares to the technical specialization specifically in [What Is a Technical Product Manager](/product-management/what-is-a-technical-product-manager).

content_md:
# Customer Discovery Process for New Products

Customer discovery is the structured process of testing whether a new product idea addresses a real, significant problem for a real group of customers — before investing significant time and money building it. It moves from an initial hypothesis, through direct customer conversations, toward real evidence of demand, following a deliberate sequence rather than jumping straight from an idea to building a full product.

## Quick facts

- Customer discovery tests whether a problem is real and significant **before** testing whether a specific solution works.
- The process typically moves through: hypothesis formation, problem interviews, solution testing, and validation.
- It connects directly to [How to Validate a Product Idea Before Building](/product-discovery/how-to-validate-a-product-idea-before-building), which covers the validation techniques used within this broader process.
- The discipline draws heavily from Steve Blank's customer development methodology, which underlies much of modern Lean Startup practice.

## The customer discovery process, step by step

1. **Form a specific, falsifiable hypothesis.** Write down exactly who you believe has a problem, what that problem is, and why you believe it's significant enough to solve — specific enough that it could actually turn out to be wrong.
2. **Run problem interviews before pitching any solution.** Talk to real potential customers about their current experience with this problem, using [open-ended, past-behavior-focused questions](/product-discovery/how-to-write-good-user-interview-questions) — without describing your product idea yet, to avoid biasing their answers.
3. **Look for evidence the problem is real and painful**, not just mildly annoying. Signs include: people currently paying for an imperfect workaround, actively searching for a solution, or describing genuine frustration with specific, concrete examples.
4. **Only then, introduce your solution concept**, and gauge reaction — ideally testing willingness to take a real, costly action (pre-order, sign up for early access with real commitment) rather than just verbal enthusiasm.
5. **Look for a pattern across multiple conversations**, not just one enthusiastic response. A single excited customer isn't validation; a repeated pattern across many independent conversations is a much stronger signal.
6. **Decide based on evidence: proceed, pivot, or abandon.** Genuine discovery requires being willing to change direction or stop, based on what the evidence actually shows, not just what you hoped to find.

## Why testing the problem comes before testing the solution

A common mistake is skipping straight to testing a solution concept, without first confirming the underlying problem is real and significant. If the problem itself isn't genuinely painful, no amount of solution refinement will produce a product people actually want — you'd be optimizing the wrong thing entirely. Customer discovery deliberately separates these two questions: first, is this a real problem worth solving; only then, is this specific solution the right way to solve it.

## What counts as real evidence during discovery

The strongest evidence comes from what people actually do, not just what they say. A person expressing polite interest ("that sounds useful") is weak evidence, since it costs them nothing to say. A person describing, unprompted, how they're currently cobbling together an imperfect workaround for this exact problem is much stronger evidence — it shows the problem is real enough that they're already investing effort to address it, even imperfectly. The strongest evidence of all comes from a costly action: a pre-order, a genuine time commitment, a willingness to switch from an existing solution.

## How customer discovery differs for an existing company vs a brand-new startup

A brand-new startup often needs to build initial customer relationships from scratch, making early discovery conversations harder to arrange but often more open and unbiased, since participants have no existing relationship or investment to color their responses. An established company doing discovery for a new product often has easier access to existing customers, but needs to be careful that existing customers' responses aren't overly polite or biased by the existing business relationship — sometimes talking to people outside the current customer base provides a more honest, unbiased signal.

## Common mistakes in the customer discovery process

- **Pitching the solution too early**, before genuinely understanding whether the underlying problem is real and significant — see the fuller list in [Common Mistakes in Customer Discovery](/product-discovery/common-mistakes-in-customer-discovery).
- **Only talking to people who are easy to reach**, like friends, colleagues, or existing enthusiastic customers, rather than a genuinely representative sample of the target market.
- **Treating polite interest as strong validation**, when it costs the respondent nothing to express and predicts real future behavior poorly.
- **Stopping discovery after just a few conversations.** A reliable pattern typically requires talking to enough people that a genuine repeated signal, not a coincidence, becomes clear.

## FAQ

**How many customer discovery interviews are enough before deciding?**
There's no universal number, but many practitioners find that 8-15 well-run problem interviews often reveal a clear pattern, with additional interviews mostly confirming rather than revealing new major themes — though this varies by how niche or broad the target market is.

**Is customer discovery only for brand-new companies, or does it apply within established companies too?**
It applies to any new product or major initiative, regardless of company age — an established company launching a genuinely new product line benefits from the same discipline of testing problem and solution assumptions before committing significant resources.

**What's the difference between customer discovery and general user research?**
Customer discovery specifically focuses on validating a new product or business idea before significant investment; broader user research includes ongoing work to understand and improve an already-existing product — the techniques overlap significantly, but the goal and stage differ.

**Can customer discovery be done without a working prototype?**
Yes, and often should be, at least in the early problem-validation stages — problem interviews and even early solution concept testing can happen with nothing built yet, using mockups, descriptions, or even just conversation, before investing in a working prototype.

content_md:
# The Design Thinking Framework for Product Teams

Design thinking is a problem-solving approach built around five stages: **Empathize**, **Define**, **Ideate**, **Prototype**, and **Test**. It's centered on a core belief: the best solutions come from deeply understanding real human needs first, generating many possible ideas before committing to one, and testing cheaply and quickly rather than building a fully finished solution based on assumptions.

## Quick facts

- The five stages: **Empathize** (understand users deeply), **Define** (frame the specific problem), **Ideate** (generate many possible solutions), **Prototype** (build a quick, testable version), **Test** (get real feedback and iterate).
- Design thinking is non-linear in practice — teams often loop back to an earlier stage as new understanding emerges.
- It shares real conceptual overlap with the [Double Diamond](/product-frameworks/double-diamond-design-process) process, both emphasizing understanding before solving.
- Popularized broadly by the design firm IDEO and Stanford's d.school.

## The five stages, explained

| Stage | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Empathize** | Deeply understand users' real needs, behaviors, and pain points through direct research |
| **Define** | Synthesize that understanding into a clear, specific problem statement |
| **Ideate** | Generate a wide range of possible solution ideas, deliberately without judging them too early |
| **Prototype** | Build a quick, low-cost, testable version of a promising idea |
| **Test** | Get real user feedback on the prototype, and use it to refine or rethink the solution |

## Why "Empathize" comes first, deliberately

Design thinking puts genuine human understanding before any solution-generating work — the belief is that solutions built without deep empathy for real user needs tend to solve the wrong problem, or solve a real problem in a way that doesn't actually fit how people really think and behave. This isn't just talking to a few users casually — it means genuinely trying to understand the emotional and practical context behind a need, often through direct observation and open-ended conversation, similar to the depth of a well-run [user interview](/product-discovery/how-to-conduct-effective-user-interviews).

## A worked example: improving a hospital's patient check-in process

**Empathize:** The team observes and talks directly to patients checking in, noticing real frustration around confusing paperwork and long waits, and to front-desk staff, noticing they're overwhelmed handling both check-in and phone calls simultaneously.

**Define:** The team frames the specific problem: "Patients feel anxious and confused during check-in because front-desk staff are too overloaded to give clear guidance."

**Ideate:** The team brainstorms broadly — a self-service check-in kiosk, a simplified paper form, a dedicated check-in-only staff role during peak hours, a pre-visit digital form completed at home, and more.

**Prototype:** The team builds a simple paper mockup of a self-service kiosk flow to test with real patients, without investing in actual kiosk hardware or software yet.

**Test:** Patients try the paper prototype, and the team observes where they get confused or hesitate, using that feedback to refine the concept before any real technical investment.

This process ensures the eventual solution is grounded in real, observed needs (overwhelmed staff, confused patients) rather than an assumption about what would help, and tests the concept cheaply before committing real engineering or hardware investment.

## Why design thinking is deliberately non-linear

Although the five stages are often presented in order, real design thinking work frequently loops back — testing a prototype might reveal the team didn't actually understand the problem as well as they thought, sending them back to Empathize or Define with new information. This non-linearity is a feature, not a flaw — it reflects the reality that genuine understanding often deepens through the process of trying to solve a problem, not just through upfront research alone.

## Design thinking vs Double Diamond

These two frameworks share substantial overlap — both prioritize deep problem understanding before solution generation, and both value exploring multiple ideas before converging. [Double Diamond](/product-frameworks/double-diamond-design-process) is often described as a simpler, four-phase structure emphasizing the diverge-converge pattern explicitly; Design thinking's five named stages place more explicit emphasis on prototyping and testing as core, named steps within the process itself, rather than folding them into a broader "Deliver" phase.

## Common mistakes when applying design thinking

- **Rushing through Empathize, relying on assumptions rather than genuine research.** This undermines the entire premise of the framework, which depends on real, deep user understanding as its foundation.
- **Judging ideas too early during Ideate**, narrowing to one idea before genuinely exploring a range of options. The value of this stage comes from deliberately deferring judgment.
- **Building an overly polished prototype**, investing more time and resources than needed just to test the core concept, defeating the purpose of testing cheaply and quickly.
- **Treating the five stages as a strict, one-way sequence.** Real design thinking work often loops back to an earlier stage — resisting this out of a desire to "finish" a stage can prevent genuinely useful iteration.

## FAQ

**Who popularized design thinking?**
The design firm IDEO and Stanford's Hasso Plattner Institute of Design (the "d.school") are widely credited with popularizing design thinking as a structured, teachable methodology, though its roots draw on earlier design and engineering problem-solving traditions.

**Is design thinking only for physical product design, or does it work for software and services too?**
It applies broadly — design thinking is used across physical products, software, services, and even organizational and business process problems, since its core discipline (deep empathy, broad ideation, cheap testing) isn't specific to any one type of output.

**How long does a full design thinking process typically take?**
It varies enormously by the scope of the problem — a focused team might move through all five stages in a few days for a smaller problem, while a complex, ambiguous challenge could take weeks or months, especially with multiple loops back through earlier stages.

**Can design thinking be combined with Agile/Scrum?**
Yes — many teams use design thinking for the discovery and problem-framing work that happens before or alongside sprint-based execution, treating it as a complementary discovery process rather than a replacement for Agile delivery practices.

title: The Double Diamond Design Process Explained

content_md:
# The Double Diamond Design Process Explained

The Double Diamond is a design process model, developed by the UK Design Council, that structures problem-solving into four phases across two cycles of "diverging" (exploring broadly) and "converging" (narrowing down to a decision): **Discover**, **Define**, **Develop**, and **Deliver**. The name comes from the shape formed when you draw these four phases — two diamonds side by side, each widening out then narrowing back in.

## Quick facts

- The four phases: **Discover** (explore the problem broadly), **Define** (narrow to a specific problem statement), **Develop** (explore solution ideas broadly), **Deliver** (narrow to a specific solution and build it).
- The core discipline is deliberately separating "exploring broadly" (diverging) from "narrowing down" (converging), rather than jumping straight to one idea.
- The first diamond focuses on understanding the *right problem*; the second diamond focuses on finding the *right solution* to that problem.
- Developed by the UK Design Council and widely adopted across design and product teams.

## The four phases, explained

| Phase | Type of thinking | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Discover** | Diverge (explore broadly) | Research broadly to understand the problem space — user needs, pain points, context |
| **Define** | Converge (narrow down) | Synthesize research into a clear, specific problem statement to solve |
| **Develop** | Diverge (explore broadly) | Generate a wide range of possible solution ideas for the defined problem |
| **Deliver** | Converge (narrow down) | Select, refine, and build the chosen solution |

## Why the "diverge then converge" pattern matters

A common mistake in problem-solving is narrowing down too quickly — jumping to the first plausible solution before genuinely exploring the problem or considering alternative approaches. The Double Diamond's explicit structure forces two distinct rounds of broad exploration before narrowing to a decision: first broadly understanding the problem before committing to a specific problem statement, then broadly generating solution ideas before committing to a specific solution. This deliberate discipline tends to produce better outcomes than skipping straight from "here's a rough problem" to "here's our solution," since it reduces the risk of solving the wrong problem, or missing a better solution that wasn't the first idea considered.

## A worked example: redesigning a checkout flow

**Discover:** The team researches broadly — reviewing analytics, watching session recordings, talking to customers who abandoned checkout — without yet committing to what the specific problem is.

**Define:** From that research, the team converges on a specific problem statement: "Customers abandon checkout most often when unexpected shipping costs appear on the final step."

**Develop:** The team broadly generates solution ideas: showing shipping costs earlier in the flow, offering a flat-rate shipping option, adding a progress indicator so users know what's coming, and a few other possibilities.

**Deliver:** The team narrows to the most promising solution — showing shipping costs earlier — refines it through prototyping and testing, and builds the final version.

Each phase has a clear purpose, and the explicit diverge-then-converge structure at both the problem and solution stages helps ensure the team didn't just solve the first problem that seemed obvious, or build the first solution idea that came to mind.

## How Double Diamond relates to Design Thinking

The Double Diamond shares real conceptual overlap with [Design Thinking](/product-frameworks/design-thinking-framework-for-product-teams) — both emphasize deeply understanding a problem before jumping to solutions, and both value generating multiple ideas before converging on one. Double Diamond is often described as a simpler, more visually memorable structure (just four phases across two diamonds), while Design Thinking typically includes more specific named stages (Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test) with a stronger emphasis on rapid prototyping and testing within the process itself.

## Common mistakes when applying Double Diamond

- **Skipping the Discover phase and starting directly at Define**, assuming the problem is already well understood without genuine research. This risks solving a problem that isn't actually the right one.
- **Not genuinely diverging during Develop**, and instead generating just one solution idea and calling it done. The value of this phase comes specifically from considering a real range of options.
- **Treating the four phases as strictly linear with no return.** In practice, teams sometimes need to revisit an earlier phase (like returning to Discover) if the Define or Develop phases reveal a gap in understanding — treating the process as too rigid can prevent this useful iteration.
- **Rushing through Discover and Develop to get to a solution faster.** The time invested in genuine divergence at both stages is what differentiates this process from simply jumping to the first idea.

## FAQ

**Who created the Double Diamond framework?**
The UK Design Council developed it, and it has since become one of the most widely referenced design process models across design and product teams internationally.

**Is Double Diamond only for visual/UX design work?**
While it originated in design practice, its underlying diverge-then-converge structure applies to a broader range of problem-solving contexts, including general product strategy and even business problem-solving beyond visual design specifically.

**How long does a full Double Diamond process typically take?**
It varies enormously by the scope of the problem — a small feature redesign might move through all four phases in a couple of weeks, while a major strategic initiative could take months, especially if the Discover phase requires extensive research.

**Can Double Diamond be used within an Agile/Scrum workflow?**
Yes — many teams use Double Diamond-style thinking for discovery work that happens before or alongside sprint execution, treating it as a discovery framework that feeds into a more traditional Agile delivery process rather than replacing it.

title: Feature Adoption Rate: How to Measure It
meta_description: Feature adoption rate shows what percentage of eligible users actually use a specific feature. See the formula, a worked example, and how to improve it.

content_md:
# Feature Adoption Rate: How to Measure It

Feature adoption rate is the percentage of eligible users who actually use a specific feature, out of everyone who could use it. It's one of the most direct ways to answer a question every product team eventually has to ask about a shipped feature: did people actually start using this, or did it launch and quietly go unused?

## Quick facts

- The formula: **Feature adoption rate = (Users who used the feature ÷ Total eligible users) × 100**
- "Eligible users" needs a clear, deliberate definition — not everyone in your whole user base necessarily should count.
- Feature adoption is usually measured over a specific time window (like 30 or 90 days after launch), not as an all-time cumulative figure.
- Low adoption doesn't automatically mean a feature is bad — it can also signal a discoverability or communication problem, not a value problem.

## The formula, and the key question behind "eligible users"

```
Feature Adoption Rate = (Users Who Used the Feature / Total Eligible Users) × 100
```

The trickiest part of this metric is defining "eligible users" correctly. If a feature is only relevant to admin-level users, including your entire user base (including non-admins) in the denominator would understate adoption misleadingly — the feature was never something most of those users could use in the first place. Getting this denominator right is essential for the resulting percentage to actually mean something useful.

## A worked example

A project management tool launches a new "recurring tasks" feature, relevant to any user with permission to create tasks (80% of the 10,000 total user base, since 20% are view-only users). Within 60 days of launch, 2,400 users have used the feature at least once.

**Feature adoption rate = 2,400 ÷ 8,000 (eligible users) × 100 = 30%**

Using the full 10,000-user base instead would have produced a misleadingly lower 24% figure, understating adoption among the users who could actually access the feature in the first place.

## Why low adoption doesn't automatically mean a feature failed

A feature with low adoption could reflect several genuinely different problems, each requiring a different fix: users don't know the feature exists (a discoverability problem, fixable with better in-product promotion), users know it exists but don't understand its value (a messaging/education problem), or users have tried it and found it doesn't actually solve their need well (a genuine product-value problem). Diagnosing which of these is actually happening — often through direct user feedback or session recordings, not just the adoption number alone — matters more than treating a low percentage as an automatic verdict on the feature's worth.

## How to actually improve feature adoption

1. **Make sure the feature is genuinely discoverable**, through in-product prompts, contextual tooltips, or release announcements — many features fail simply because users never noticed they exist.
2. **Clearly communicate the specific value**, not just that the feature exists — explain what problem it solves and why a user should care, in language tied to their actual workflow.
3. **Reduce friction to try it.** If using the feature for the first time requires significant setup or configuration, that friction alone can suppress adoption regardless of the feature's underlying value.
4. **Talk directly to users who haven't adopted it**, to understand whether the barrier is awareness, understanding, or genuine lack of fit — each requires a different response.
5. **Re-measure after making changes**, to confirm whether your adoption-improvement efforts actually worked, rather than assuming they did.

## Feature adoption rate vs overall product adoption

Feature adoption rate is specific to one feature; broader "product adoption" often refers to overall usage of the core product itself. A product can have strong overall adoption (people use the core product regularly) while individual features within it have widely varying adoption rates — some heavily used, others barely touched. Tracking feature-level adoption specifically reveals which parts of the product are actually delivering value versus quietly going unused, information a single blended product-level metric would hide.

## Common mistakes when measuring feature adoption

- **Using the entire user base as the denominator when only a subset of users are actually eligible for the feature.** This understates true adoption among the people who could realistically use it.
- **Measuring adoption too soon after launch**, before users have had realistic time to discover and try the feature.
- **Treating "used once" the same as genuine, ongoing adoption.** A user who tried a feature once and never returned is meaningfully different from one who's incorporated it into regular use — some teams track both one-time trial and repeat usage as separate signals.
- **Not investigating the reason behind low adoption before deciding a feature failed.** As covered above, low adoption can stem from several different causes, each requiring a different response.

## FAQ

**How soon after launch should feature adoption be measured?**
It depends on how frequently the feature would naturally be used — a daily-use feature can be assessed within a couple of weeks, while a less frequently needed feature might need a longer window (60-90 days) to give users a realistic chance to encounter and try it.

**What's a good feature adoption rate?**
There's no universal benchmark — it varies enormously based on how core or niche the feature is to the product's main use case. Comparing adoption across similar features within your own product, and tracking trends over time, is more useful than comparing to a generic external number.

**Should feature adoption be tracked as one-time use or repeated use?**
Both are valuable and answer different questions — one-time trial rate shows whether people are willing to try it at all; repeat usage rate shows whether it's actually becoming a genuine, sustained part of their workflow.

**Is feature adoption rate the same as feature usage frequency?**
No — adoption rate measures what percentage of eligible users use a feature at all; usage frequency measures how often those adopting users actually use it once they've started — both are useful, but they answer different questions.

faq.answer: No — adoption rate measures what percentage of eligible users use a feature at all; usage frequency measures how often those adopting users actually use it once they've started — both are useful, but they answer different questions.

title: First Principles Thinking in Product Management

primary_keyword: first principles thinking in product management
secondary_keywords: reasoning by analogy vs first principles
content_md:
# First Principles Thinking in Product Management

First principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic, fundamental truths, and reasoning up from there — instead of reasoning by analogy, where you assume something is true simply because it resembles how things have always been done or how a competitor does it. For a product manager, this means questioning the underlying assumptions behind "that's just how this works" and asking what's actually, fundamentally true about the problem, independent of existing conventions.

## Quick facts

- **Reasoning by analogy:** basing a decision on how similar things have been done before ("competitors all do X, so we should too").
- **First principles reasoning:** breaking a problem down to its fundamental, verifiable truths, and building a solution up from those truths directly.
- First principles thinking is more time- and effort-intensive, but can surface genuinely novel solutions analogy-based reasoning tends to miss.
- It's especially valuable when an entire industry seems stuck following the same convention, potentially due to inherited assumptions nobody has actually re-examined.

## The core difference, illustrated

| | Reasoning by Analogy | First Principles Thinking |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | "How do others solve this?" | "What's fundamentally true about this problem?" |
| Typical output | A solution similar to existing approaches | Potentially a genuinely different approach |
| Speed | Faster — leverages existing patterns | Slower — requires deeper, more deliberate analysis |
| Risk | May inherit unnecessary assumptions from existing approaches | Higher effort, and not every problem benefits from this depth |

## A classic example: Elon Musk and rocket costs

The most commonly cited example of first principles thinking comes from Elon Musk's approach to rocket costs at SpaceX. The conventional, analogy-based reasoning in the aerospace industry was "rockets are expensive because that's just how much rockets cost, based on historical prices." Musk instead asked a first-principles question: what are rockets actually made of, and what does that raw material actually cost? He found the raw materials cost a small fraction of a rocket's typical price — revealing that the high cost was largely a function of manufacturing and reuse practices, not some fundamental, unavoidable truth about rockets — which directly informed SpaceX's strategy around reusable rockets.

## A worked example in product management

Picture a team building a customer onboarding flow, where the industry convention is a 5-7 step signup wizard, since "that's how everyone does onboarding." Reasoning by analogy would mean building a similar 5-7 step wizard. First principles thinking instead asks: what's fundamentally required before a user can get real value from this product? If the honest answer is "just an email and one piece of information," then the industry-standard multi-step wizard may be carrying unnecessary assumptions inherited from other products' specific needs, not a fundamental requirement of onboarding in general. This kind of reasoning can lead to a genuinely simpler, more differentiated onboarding experience than simply copying the convention.

## When first principles thinking is worth the extra effort

This approach is most valuable when a whole market or industry seems to follow the same convention without a clear, examined reason — a strong signal that reasoning by analogy has taken over collective practice, and a genuine opportunity might exist for whoever questions it first. It's less necessary for well-understood, low-stakes decisions where existing patterns are well-tested and there's little reason to believe they're carrying unnecessary assumptions — reserving deep first-principles analysis for genuinely important, potentially convention-bound problems is usually the better use of the extra effort it requires.

## How to actually practice first principles thinking

1. **Identify the assumption you're about to make by analogy.** "We should do X because that's how it's usually done" is the signal to pause.
2. **Ask what's fundamentally, verifiably true about the underlying problem**, stripped of any assumption inherited from existing solutions.
3. **Build a solution up from those fundamental truths**, rather than starting from an existing pattern and adjusting it slightly.
4. **Sanity-check the result against practical constraints** — first principles thinking can surface a theoretically elegant solution that's still impractical given real business or technical constraints, so the final step still requires practical judgment.

## Common mistakes with first principles thinking

- **Applying it to every decision, regardless of stakes.** This is genuinely time-intensive — reserving it for higher-stakes decisions where convention seems questionable is a better use of the effort.
- **Mistaking contrarianism for first principles thinking.** The goal is genuinely examining fundamental truths, not simply doing the opposite of convention for its own sake.
- **Ignoring practical constraints once a first-principles solution is identified.** An elegant, fundamentally-reasoned solution still needs to survive contact with real business, technical, and resource constraints.
- **Not validating the fundamental assumptions you're building from.** First principles thinking is only as good as the accuracy of the "fundamental truths" it starts from — if those are wrong, the whole chain of reasoning is undermined.

## FAQ

**Is first principles thinking always better than reasoning by analogy?**
No — reasoning by analogy is faster and often perfectly adequate for well-understood, lower-stakes decisions. First principles thinking is more valuable specifically when convention seems questionable or when a genuinely novel solution could create real competitive advantage.

**Does first principles thinking always lead to a different conclusion than convention?**
Not necessarily — sometimes deep first-principles analysis confirms that the conventional approach actually is the right one for good, fundamental reasons, which is itself valuable to know with more confidence than assuming it by default.

**How is first principles thinking different from the 5 Whys technique?**
[5 Whys](/business-analyst/how-to-do-root-cause-analysis-5-whys-fishbone) is specifically a root-cause analysis technique for understanding why a problem occurred. First principles thinking is a broader reasoning approach applicable to design and strategy decisions generally, not limited to root-cause analysis.

**Can first principles thinking be practiced as a team, or is it more of an individual skill?**
It works well as a group exercise — explicitly asking "what's the industry-standard assumption here, and is it actually fundamentally true?" as a team discussion can surface useful challenges to convention that a single person might not think to question alone.
